3.0.s.en: (1) Solomon allies himself by marriage with Pharaoh and sacrifices on the high places

3.0.0.en: Pharaoh king of Egypt: he is Siamun, one of the kings of the Twenty-first Dynasty, who reigned from the year

3.0.2.en: The city of David: a part of Jerusalem, and then the name was applied to all of Jerusalem.

3.0.3.en: The house of the Lord: Solomon began its foundation in the fourth year of his reign and it took seven years, that is, he completed it in the eleventh year of his reign, and after that he began to build his own house, that is, his palaces (ch. 6:1, 38). His own house: Solomon built a group of palaces for himself over a period of 13 years (ch. 7:1), that is, he completed them in the twenty-fourth year of his reign.

3.0.4.en: The wall of Jerusalem: Solomon built a new wall for the city surrounding the new buildings he had erected, and he also repaired the old wall (ch. 11:27).

3.0.5.en: Solomon thought, with human wisdom, to ally himself by marriage with Pharaoh king of Egypt, for the sake of the standing and power of Egypt, and in this he broke the Law by marrying a pagan woman (Ex 34:16; Deut 7:3). Indeed, he later married other pagan women who had a role in turning him away from the worship of God, so his marriage alliance with Pharaoh was the beginning of the errors into which he fell. He built her a house outside Jerusalem, in which she lived temporarily until he completed building his palaces inside Jerusalem and also built the house of the Lord and the walls of the city.

3.0.6.en: Some see that Solomon's marriage to Pharaoh's daughter did not draw him to the worship of idols, as proved by the fact that he did not set up statues of the Egyptian gods when he built high places for the gods of his foreign wives (ch. 11:1-8), and perhaps she converted to Judaism after her marriage; but this does not negate Solomon's error in marrying a pagan woman.

3.1.0.en: The high places: the mountains or high hills.

3.1.1.en: The tabernacle of meeting at that time was in Gibeon, and in it was the bronze altar on which the sacrifices and burnt offerings to the Lord were offered. However, the people were not committed to offering sacrifices in one specific place until after the building of the Temple, so until that time they offered their sacrifices on any high place. This was a lack of exactness on their part, although Gideon and Samuel offered sacrifices in places other than the tabernacle of meeting as an exception (Judg 6:26; 1 Sam 9:12). And Solomon himself was not committed to offering sacrifices at the tabernacle of meeting, as the Lord commanded (Deut 12:1-14), as David his father was.

3.1.2.en: Because the people offered sacrifices so often on the high places, they called the tabernacle of meeting at Gibeon "the great high place" (v. 4), meaning that they offered sacrifices on any high place like the pagans.

3.2.0.en: Although Solomon was careful to please the Lord and to do the rites and prayers his father had followed, he shared with the people in sacrificing on the high places. This was a disregard on his part, because God commanded that sacrifices be offered in one place, the tabernacle of meeting, and this later helped lead to offering sacrifices to the idols that Solomon set up, in violation of the law of God, because he was not committed to offering sacrifices only at the tabernacle of meeting like his father David.

3.3.0.en: Gibeon: it lies northwest of Jerusalem at a distance of 8 km, and is in the portion of the tribe of Benjamin, and was afterward given to the priests. It gained special fame because David placed the tabernacle of meeting and the bronze altar there (1 Chr 16:39; 21:29; 2 Chr 1:3-6). Before Solomon began to carry out his work in the kingdom, he cared for the worship of God, so he went to the altar of the Lord at Gibeon, where the tabernacle of meeting and the bronze altar were, and there Solomon offered many burnt offerings. The Scripture mentions that he offered a thousand burnt offerings; most likely they were not all offered on one day, because the bronze altar could not accommodate offering this number in one day, but it took several days.

3.3.1.en: Solomon's offering of a great number of sacrifices shows:

3.3.2.en: 1- The extent of Solomon's love for God and his generosity in giving to Him.

3.3.4.en: One of the important things we must hold fast to is to give God the first place in our lives, so that we are not troubled by our daily cares, but lift up our hearts to God before we carry out our daily work, or any new work we undertake. God is the only One able to lead us in the wilderness of this world so that we reach the shore of safety in the bosom of His saints.

3.4.0.en: In response to Solomon's love, which he showed at Gibeon, the Lord appeared to him in a dream and blessed him for his love and encouraged him, and said to him, "Ask what I shall give thee." For God rejoices in the gifts of His children, and so He repays them with abundant gifts according to the abundance of His riches.

3.4.1.en: We notice that God cares for man's freedom, so He lets him choose the request he wants from Him: "Ask what I shall give thee."

3.4.2.en: In His love, God wants to give us generously all that we need, and rejoices that we ask and persist before Him. I wish that you would trust in God's love and ask for your needs, especially the spiritual ones, so that you may be satisfied by Him and abide in Him.

3.5.0.en: Solomon thanked God for His mercy which He poured out on David his father, because he walked with God, and this mercy grew greater in setting his son as king to sit on his throne.

3.6.0.en: I know not how to go out or come in: I do not know how to act in the external affairs of the kingdom, in dealing with other peoples, and I do not know how to act in its internal affairs. When Solomon thanked God for making him king, he confessed humbly before Him that he was little. Being at the beginning of his twenties, he did not know how to act in the kingdom and how to manage its affairs, especially since the people of the children of Israel were great in number and so needed wisdom and strength in leading them. Solomon felt that he was a steward over the people of God, and so he says "thy people," for God is the true King.

3.7.0.en: Because of Solomon's sense of his weakness and the great number of the people, he asked God for wisdom, understanding, and the ability to discern, in order to lead this great people and to act well in all their affairs.

3.8.0.en: God was pleased because Solomon did not ask for material things and earthly desires such as long life, or riches, or victory over enemies, but asked for wisdom to fulfill his duty in leading the people under God's guidance. Therefore God gave him wisdom more than all men, not only in his own time, but no one before him had attained it, nor would anyone after him. This wisdom is knowledge, understanding, and exceedingly great intelligence, and it is human wisdom; but man must submit with this wisdom to God and His commandments, and so receive spiritual wisdom. Sadly, Solomon did not hold to this, so he broke the Law and multiplied marriages, horses, and chariots, and made idols for his pagan wives.

3.9.0.en: In addition to what Solomon asked, the Lord promised that he would also receive what he did not ask, riches and honor which no other king among his contemporaries would attain.

3.10.0.en: God promised Solomon length of days on condition of walking in His way and keeping His commandments as David his father walked and did; but sadly, in spite of Solomon's goodness and his great accomplishments such as building the Temple, he established the worship of idols in Jerusalem, so his life was not prolonged, and he lived only sixty years.

3.11.0.en: His servants: the chief workers with him.

3.11.1.en: When Solomon awoke from his dream, he rejoiced greatly at the vision of God and His great promises to him, so he went to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant of God and thanked Him, to declare that his kingship and wisdom were from God and not from himself or from the people. He offered many peace offerings and made a feast for his servants so that they might share with him in his joy, since the one who offers peace offerings and his loved ones share in eating of them.

3.11.2.en: Here we see Solomon as a spiritual leader who takes care to make his helpers, the servants working with him, share in the spiritual joy, for he related to them what had happened in the dream, and they thanked God and submitted to His commandments.

3.11.3.en: I wish that you would make spiritual requests and ask for God's help to fulfill your responsibilities before you ask for material needs. Your God is able to do all things, but He rejoices when He finds your spiritual desires and your love for Him to be great.

3.12.0.en: This incident tells us of the first manifestation of Solomon's wisdom which God gave him. Two harlots came to the king, each with a complaint against the other. Of course, this case was first presented to the judges and elders, and they were perplexed about resolving it, so they referred it to Solomon to decide it because of his distinction in wisdom.

3.13.0.en: One of them began to relate to him the problem between them, which was that she and the other woman lived in one dwelling that no other person shared with them, and both of them had borne a child, with a difference of only three days between them.

3.14.0.en: The woman continued her story and said that the other woman's son died in the night because she - by an unintentional mistake - lay on him. So what she did was to rise in the night, when she realized what had happened, and slip in to where I was sleeping and exchange the two children, putting her dead son in place of the living son, whom she took from me, and she went to her bed.

3.15.0.en: The woman completes the story and says that when she woke in the morning and prepared to nurse the child, she found him dead, and when she looked closely at him she realized that he was not her son whom she had borne.

3.16.0.en: At this point in the story the two women began to cry out in each other's faces. The other woman objects and says that her son is the living one and that this woman's son is the dead one, and this one answers her and says, No, rather your son is the dead one and mine is the living. They kept repeating and restating the same words while in the presence of King Solomon.

3.17.0.en: The king showed the difficulty of the problem, since each of them declares that her son is the living one ... So what, one wonders, is the solution?!

3.18.0.en: Here the wisdom with which God had favored the king was manifested, for he asked those around him for a sword, and they brought it to him at once.

3.19.0.en: In order that Solomon might discover the true mother, he said to them, since you are disputing over this child, let him be cut in two and let each one take half.

3.20.0.en: Her bowels yearned: the heart of the true mother was inflamed for her son.

3.20.1.en: The true mother could not bear the killing of her son before her eyes, so she begged the king that they give the child to the other woman, while the other insisted on what the king had declared, that the child be cut in two, and her evil appeared in her attempt to be rid of the son as her own son had died.

3.21.0.en: From the reaction of the two women to the order to divide the child, Solomon was able to know the true mother, so he issued a judgment to give the child to his true mother and not to kill him.

3.22.0.en: Here everyone realized the wisdom of the king, after they had wondered at his judgment to divide the child, asking how the king could order the killing of a living child and the depriving of both women of him.

3.22.1.en: By this judgment Solomon gained the esteem and veneration of the people, for they truly felt from his judgment in this problem that God had given him wisdom, to execute just judgments among the members of his people.

3.22.2.en: We notice that although the two women were harlots, Solomon did not refuse to arbitrate between them because of their evil, but issued a just judgment.

3.22.3.en: God is ready to give you discernment and wisdom in all your affairs, with a simplicity and power that astonish those around you. Only rely on Him and seek Him, and He will guide you in all your steps.

3.22.4.en: The wisdom of Solomon and the greatness of his kingdom

4.0.0.en: All Israel: because the kingdom expanded in his days to its farthest limits, reaching from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates.

4.0.1.en: Solomon was distinguished in his management of the kingdom, so he appointed officials in every sector to manage the affairs of the kingdom, as mentioned in these verses.

4.0.2.en: Azariah the son of Zadok the priest: he was the grandson of Zadok and the son of Ahimaaz (1 Chr 6:9). He is attributed as the son of Zadok because of Zadok's fame. He was one of the senior officials in the reign of Solomon. The writer of the book did not mention the post he was entrusted with, but his appearing at the head of the list suggests that he was regarded as the first official, that is, a chief minister or prime minister, in addition to his priestly work. He may have been the priest in Gibeon before the building of the house of the Lord was completed, while Zadok was in Jerusalem.

4.0.3.en: Elihoreph and Ahiah the sons of Shisha: scribes, that is, they recorded the laws of the state and did secretarial work. Shisha, their father, who is also called Shavsha and Sheva in (2 Sam 20:25) and Seraiah in (2 Sam 8:17), was a scribe to King David and to Solomon after him, and his two sons inherited this post from him.

4.0.4.en: Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud: he held the post of recorder in the reigns of both David and Solomon, as mentioned in (2 Sam 8:16 and 20:24 and 1 Chr 18:15), and his task was to keep records of contemporary events as a record of history.

4.0.5.en: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada: one of the commanders of the army from the days of David, famous for his courage (2 Sam 23:20-23). He was a faithful friend to Solomon who stood by his side against Adonijah's rebellion, and after Joab was killed he took his place at the head of the army. He was also responsible for protecting the royal palace and the king, that is, he was like the commander of the royal guard.

4.0.6.en: Zadok and Abiathar: Zadok is the son of Ahitub, of the descendants of Eleazar the son of Aaron. He was one of the two great priests in the days of David, and Abiathar, who is also called Ahimelech, was the other priest (2 Sam 8:17). When Adonijah wanted to seize the kingship, Zadok remained faithful to David, but Abiathar sided with Adonijah, so Solomon expelled him from the priesthood and Zadok alone remained the great priest.

4.0.7.en: It is noticed that the name of Abiathar appears as high priest together with Zadok although Solomon had removed him. This is explained by the fact that Solomon prevented him from practicing the priestly work but left him the title without the work, in appreciation of his previous great services in the days of David his father and because he was anointed as a priest.

4.0.8.en: Azariah the son of Nathan: he is also called Azariah. He is the son of the brother of King Solomon, that is, Solomon was his uncle; Solomon appointed him overseer over the twelve officers who will be mentioned in detail (vv. 7-19). Zabud the son of Nathan: he is the son of Nathan the prophet. He was a close friend of Solomon and so was called a priest, not in the sense that he served as a priest in the Temple of God, but because he was close to the king as the priest is close to God. The same meaning was said before in (2 Sam 8:18) that David's sons were priests, that is, close to the king and his helpers. And it was mentioned that he was a priest and the king's friend, that is, he was an adviser to the king and one of those close to him.

4.0.9.en: Ahishar: an official in charge of the affairs of Solomon's house, as Joseph was over the house of Potiphar, distinguished in his ordering of the house, so that the queen of Sheba was greatly impressed by the ordering of Solomon's house (ch. 10). Adoniram the son of Abda: he is the same as Adoram mentioned in (2 Sam 20:24), and is also called Hadoram in (2 Chr 10:18). He remained in his post throughout the reign of Solomon and Rehoboam, and he is the one whom Rehoboam king of Judah sent to Israel, and the children of Israel stoned him with stones and he died. He was responsible for putting people to work on state projects by forced labor, that is, without pay, such as the building of the house of the Lord, and then the king's house, and he gave them only their food, so he was hated by the people, and therefore his life ended in death by stoning.

4.0.10.en: We see that the administrative organization in the reign of Solomon took first place before the military organization, because peace prevailed in his reign, which gave him an opportunity to advance the kingdom, unlike David, in whose days wars were many and the kingdom accordingly expanded at his hands.

4.0.11.en: Managing any work needs order, so I wish that you would manage your own affairs and your work with order, distributing responsibilities and not interfering in everything yourself, lest you cancel the responsibilities of those around you and become burdened with responsibilities.

4.1.0.en: They provided food: gathered food, and the word "mira" means food.

4.1.1.en: The king appointed twelve officers, each over a region of the lands of the children of Israel, to gather food for the king's house. What is meant by the king's house is the households belonging to him and the feasts he gave for his helpers and guests, which were a great deal. These officers gathered it without charge from the people, and the people were content because of the abundance of good things with which God had blessed them in the days of Solomon. Each officer gathered food from his region to supply the needs of the king's house one month of the year, that is, the year was divided among twelve officers. The names of the officers and the districts they were responsible for:

4.1.2.en: The officer, the district: 10B - the son of Hur, Mount Ephraim 1B. The land of the tribe of Ephraim, extending from Jerusalem to Jezreel. It was later called Samaria.

4.1.3.en: 213B - the son of Deker, Makaz and Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh and Elon-beth-hanan 2B. Shaalbim or Shaalbin: a city in the tribe of Dan.

4.1.4.en: Beth-shemesh: a city in the portion of the tribe of Issachar.

4.1.5.en: Elon-beth-hanan: a town in the portion of the tribe of Dan.

4.1.6.en: 314B - the son of Hesed 3B. Aruboth and Sochoh and all the land of Hepher, which is in the plain of Sharon, and these are lands west of the Jordan, southwest of Jerusalem.

4.1.7.en: 415B - the son of Abinadab, all the region of Dor 4B. Son-in-law of the king, he married the daughter of Solomon. Dor: a city on the Mediterranean Sea, 13 km north of Caesarea, and its name is "Tafah"; it was given to the tribe of Manasseh.

4.1.8.en: Solomon used to encourage marriages between his assistants and his daughters, because this ensures the political stability of the kingdom. 516B - Baana the son of Ahilud, Taanach and Megiddo and all Beth-shean, which is beside Zarethan, below Jezreel 5B. He is also the brother of Jehoshaphat. From Beth-shean to Abel-meholah, as far as the place beyond Jokneam.

4.1.9.en: The recorder. Taanach: the mound of Taanach, which lies on the southern edge of the plain of Jezreel, that is, in the middle of Israel.

4.1.10.en: Megiddo: it lies 30 km southeast of Haifa in the tribe of Issachar.

4.1.11.en: Beth-shean: a city 8 km west of the Jordan River, attached to the tribe of Manasseh.

4.1.12.en: Zarethan: a village east of Jezreel in the land of the tribe of Manasseh.

4.1.13.en: Jezreel: a triangular plain in the middle of the land of the children of Israel.

4.1.15.en: The place beyond Jokneam: a city adjacent to the Jordan River on its western bank.

4.1.16.en: 617B - the son of Geber 6B. Ramoth-gilead, the towns of Jair the son of Manasseh, which are in Gilead, and the region of Argob, which is in Bashan: threescore great cities with walls and brasen bars.

4.1.17.en: Ramoth-gilead: that is, the heights of Gilead, a city of the tribe of Gad east of the Jordan.

4.1.18.en: The towns of Jair the son of Manasseh: a group of villages in the northwestern part of Bashan.

4.1.19.en: Gilead: a mountainous region east of the Jordan (half of Mount Gilead was given to Reuben and Gad and the rest of Gilead to the half tribe of Manasseh.

4.1.20.en: Argob: a region in Bashan that included 60 fortified cities (Deut 3:4), which Jair the son of Manasseh took, so the place was called Havoth-jair, that is, the village of Jair or the villages of the sons of Manasseh.

4.1.21.en: 718B - Ahinadab the son of Iddo 7B. Mahanaim, a city east of the Jordan, half of it belonging to Gad and the other half to Manasseh, north of the river Jabbok.

4.1.22.en: 819B - Ahimaaz, Naphtali 8B, the son of Zadok the high priest. The lands of the tribe of Naphtali.

4.1.23.en: In the days of David, he used to inform him of the plans of Absalom.

4.1.24.en: He married "Basmath" the daughter of Solomon"

4.1.25.en: 920B - Baanah the son of Hushai 9B. Asher and Aloth: he is the son of Hushai the Archite. Aloth: a place in the portion of Asher.

4.1.26.en: The wise and faithful counselor of David who scattered the counsel of Ahithophel.

4.1.27.en: 1021B - Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah, Issachar 10B. 1122B - Shimei the son of Elah, Benjamin 11B. A Benjamite, one of David's mighty men.

4.1.28.en: 1223B - Geber the son of Uri 12B. The southern part of the land of Gilead; the land of Gilead is east of the Jordan and was originally that of Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan.

4.1.29.en: Solomon's wisdom is noticed in placing Geber and his son (vv. 13, 19) as officers over two adjacent districts, to make cooperation between them easy, so that Solomon would reach better results from their work. We also find that nine officers worked west of the Jordan and only three were east of the Jordan, because of the smallness of the area belonging to the people of God there. These three officers are the son of Geber (v. 13), Ahinadab (v. 14), and Geber the son of Uri (v. 19). Over all these officers was one general overseer, Azariah the son of Nathan, as stated in v. 5.

4.1.30.en: It is recorded of Solomon here, along with his wisdom, his ability to organize the state, for he appointed to each responsibility the person suited to it, so that everything went in right order. We too, along with our submission and our faith in the blessing of the Lord in the ordering of things, must manage the affairs of our life and organize our matters with prudence and wisdom, and then leave the Lord to accomplish every matter according to His will.

4.2.0.en: It is mentioned here that the people of God were very many, and the tribe of Judah is singled out for mention because it occupied a large area and from it came David, from whose descendants Christ came. Thus God's promise to Abraham of a multitude of descendants was fulfilled (Gen 22:17), and an abundance of good things, so they were in continual joy.

4.2.1.en: The increase in number in the days of Solomon was a symbol of the increase of the descendants of Abraham who would believe in Christ in the whole world in the New Testament.

4.3.0.en: The divine promise to the people of God was likewise fulfilled, for Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the great river, that is, the river Euphrates, to the river of Egypt, which lies at its border near El-Arish, and it is a seasonal river of flood waters in Sinai and not the Nile. The compulsory gifts, which were considered as tribute from the people, were a cause of the increase in the state's resources, in addition to the fact that forced labor provided the state with much money.

4.4.0.en: Measure (cor): a measure equal to 229 liters.

4.4.2.en: Harts: plural of hind, a kind of deer.

4.4.3.en: Fallowdeer: animals of the deer family.

4.4.4.en: Roebucks: the singular is roebuck, which is the gazelle.

4.4.5.en: What the palace and those living in it, those granted the honor of sitting at the king's table, and the guests and great invitees required was a large quantity of food and drink in one day, as follows: 30 measures of fine flour, 60 measures of meal, 10 fat oxen, 20 oxen out of the pastures, 100 sheep, and large numbers of harts, animals, and fatted fowl.

4.4.6.en: This means that Solomon's table sufficed to feed about 4000 persons, and he here is a type of Christ, who satisfied 4000 persons with seven loaves and a few small fishes.

4.5.0.en: This side the river: the lands lying west of the river Euphrates.

4.5.1.en: Tiphsah: an anciently known city lying west of the river Euphrates.

4.5.2.en: Gaza: a well-known city on the Mediterranean Sea near the border of Egypt.

4.5.3.en: Dan: it lies at the far north of the land of the Jews.

4.5.4.en: Beersheba: a city lying at the far south of Judea.

4.5.5.en: In the days of Solomon the promises of the Lord to the fathers were fulfilled, for his authority extended from the river Euphrates in the east to the Mediterranean Sea and the border of Egypt in the west, and from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south, and all the kings of the countries surrounding his kingdom submitted to him and made peace with him and gave him gifts and money. So the children of Israel, that is, the tribe of Judah and the rest of the tribes, lived in peace, enjoying the good things of the rich land such as vines and figs. The tribe of Judah is mentioned because of its large number and not because it was divided from the rest of the tribes in the days of Solomon.

4.5.6.en: The people of God were satisfied and safe in the days of Solomon, and Solomon is a type of the believers in the New Testament over whom Christ reigns, so they enjoy spiritual satisfaction and peace.

4.6.0.en: Stall: the place set apart for putting the animals' food in.

4.6.1.en: Solomon's wealth is shown here, for he had forty thousand stalls for feeding his horses, and he also had twelve thousand horsemen to ride these horses. The multiplying of horses is contrary to the Law, because God wanted them to rely on Him and not on their military strength through a multitude of horsemen and horses (Deut 17:16).

4.7.1.en: The officers previously appointed over the twelve districts supplied the needs of the royal palace - as mentioned before - each in his month, so the palace lacked nothing. Those responsible for supplying straw and barley brought it to the officers of the districts to send it to feed the king's horses, according to the times set for it, so that there would be food throughout the year for these animals.

4.7.2.en: I wish that you would thank God for the good things He prepares for you, so you enjoy them, for they are precious because they are from God, and so rejoice in God's love for you and give to the needy, and then the little that you have becomes much, and you are content, thankful, and loving to give.

4.8.0.en: God's grace to Solomon was very great, for his wisdom was great beyond all measure and he knew many things in various kinds of knowledge and was ready, with a wide heart, to solve all the problems brought to him, so that he expresses the breadth of his wisdom and heart by the sand of the sea, which cannot be counted; so varied were the knowledge and learning by which he was distinguished.

4.8.1.en: Long-suffering is a great virtue, so I wish that you would care for it, and so listen well to everyone around you however weak they are in expressing themselves, encouraging them with your smile, giving rest to their hearts, so that they find Christ in you.

4.9.0.en: The children of the east country: they were distinguished by wisdom, like the friends of Job and the magi and the Chaldeans in the days of Daniel.

4.9.1.en: The wisdom of Egypt: Egypt was famous for wise men, as it was in the days of Joseph and Moses.

4.9.2.en: Ethan the Ezrahite: from the clan of Zerah of the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 2:6), famous for his wisdom, and he is the writer of the three sons of Mahol:

4.9.3.en: Heman: the son of Mahol the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, known for his great wisdom, and he is the composer of Psalm 88.

4.9.4.en: Chalcol: the son of Mahol, who was also among the wisest men of his time (1 Chr 2:6). Darda: the son of Mahol, who was also famous for wisdom (1 Chr 2:6). Of course there were wise men in various parts of the earth, whether among the children of the east or in Egypt, but the wisdom that Solomon enjoyed surpassed the wisdom of all these. His wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all men, among them Ethan the Ezrahite and Heman and Chalcol and Darda the sons of Mahol. And his fame and wisdom spread in all the surrounding nations.

4.10.0.en: Solomon's wisdom appeared in the many proverbs he uttered, which numbered three thousand proverbs, and in the songs he composed, which numbered a thousand and five. Some of these proverbs and songs were placed in the Book of Proverbs in the Holy Bible. We also know that the Book of Proverbs is not all the work of Solomon, as is written in the book.

4.11.0.en: Hyssop: a small plant that climbs on rocks and walls, from which bunches are made that are used in Jewish rites to dip in blood and sprinkle with. Some see that it is the thyme plant. Creeping things: reptiles.

4.11.1.en: His knowledge reached to understanding the properties of the earth and the world of plants, and he described many kinds of them, from the cedar of Lebanon to the hyssop that springs out of the wall, that is, from the greatest trees such as the cedar to the smallest plants such as hyssop. As his knowledge of the plant kingdom surpassed the limits of the knowledge of all his contemporaries, so his description of the beasts, birds, reptiles, and fishes was complete and exact.

4.12.0.en: When Solomon's surpassing knowledge appeared and news of it spread among the kingdoms of the world, kings and leaders of the world came to meet him and to enjoy hearing and seeing his wisdom.

4.12.1.en: Seize every opportunity to learn from the wisdom of others and to be a disciple at the hands of spiritual brothers, for because of your love of wisdom and your humility God pours out much upon you and you enjoy His work in you.
